entries.name: Granite
entries.notes: The continents' foundation. The world's most-quarried dimension stone; half of all obelisks are granite.

entries.name: Basalt
entries.notes: Covers most of the ocean floor. Column-jointed flows give hexagonal pillars (Giant's Causeway); the Deccan and Siberian Traps are flood basalts.

entries.name: Andesite
entries.notes: The signature rock of subduction zones, named for the Andes. Inca masonry at Cusco and Machu Picchu is andesite, cut to fit without mortar.

entries.name: Rhyolite
entries.notes: The volcanic equivalent of granite: silica-rich and explosive-prone. Yellowstone's domes are rhyolite; its glassy form is obsidian.

entries.name: Gabbro
entries.notes: Coarse-grained basalt equivalent; forms the lower oceanic crust. 'Black Galaxy' granites sold for countertops are gabbro.

entries.name: Diorite
entries.notes: Salt-and-pepper intermediate rock, darker than granite, with little or no quartz. Trade stones sold as 'black granite' are often diorite.

entries.name: Obsidian
entries.notes: Volcanic glass with no crystals; conchoidal fracture gives edges sharper than steel. Hydration rinds are used to date artifacts.

entries.name: Pumice
entries.notes: Frothed silica melt, 64-85% voids; it floats. Krakatoa's 1883 blast sent pumice rafts drifting across the Indian Ocean for years.

entries.name: Tuff
entries.notes: Consolidated volcanic ash. Easter Island's moai were carved from Rano Raraku tuff; Romans burned it into building mortar.

entries.name: Granodiorite
entries.notes: The backbone of many cordilleras (e.g. Sierra Nevada); most 'granites' by trade name are really granodiorite.

entries.name: Tonalite
entries.notes: The quartz-poor diorite of arc batholiths; a major component of continental crust generation at subduction zones.

entries.name: Dacite
entries.notes: Intermediate-silica lava that barely flows; the May 1980 Mount St. Helens blast was dacite, and its domes still grow slowly.

entries.name: Diabase (dolerite)
entries.notes: Medium-grained basalt equivalent, crystallized in dikes and sills. The 'traprock' of the quarry industry; extremely tough and common.

entries.name: Syenite
entries.notes: Granite without quartz, named after Syene (Aswan), whose red syenite built obelisks. Larvikite is a ternary-feldspar variety.

entries.name: Monzonite
entries.notes: Halfway between granite and syenite, with roughly equal plagioclase and alkali feldspar. Named for the Monzoni range in the Italian Alps.

entries.name: Scoria
entries.notes: Vesicular mafic rock; cinder cones are built of it. Easter Island's red scoria topknots came from the Puna Pau quarry.

entries.name: Ignimbrite
entries.notes: Deposit of a nuée ardente: hot ash welding itself into rock. Its sheared pumice streaks are called fiamme; Yucca Mountain is excavated in welded ignimbrite.

entries.name: Perlite
entries.notes: Obsidian that drank 2-5% water; heated, it pops like popcorn into 10-20x white granules used in potting mix and plaster.

entries.name: Trachyte
entries.notes: The silica-poor relative of rhyolite, common in the East African Rift and the Rhineland volcanic fields; many German millstones were cut from trachyte.

entries.name: Latite
entries.notes: Coarse equivalent of monzonite: plagioclase plus alkali feldspar without free quartz. Named for Latium, the ancient region around Rome.

entries.name: Phonolite
entries.notes: From the Greek phone, 'sound': slabs ring like a bell when struck. Common in East African Rift volcanoes such as those around Nairobi.

entries.name: Anorthosite
entries.notes: Nearly pure plagioclase; it builds the lunar highlands. Proterozoic massifs crop out in the Adirondacks and Labrador (source of labradorite/spectrolite).

entries.name: Pegmatite
uses: lithium, tantalum, beryllium and cesium ore
entries.notes: The last, water-rich granitic fluid freezes into crystals metres across. Primary source of most rare elements on Earth; mineable crystals here.

entries.name: Larvikite
entries.notes: Norway's national stone, from the Oslo Rift near Larvik. Lamellae in its blue-grey feldspar scatter light for a shifting blue flash.

entries.name: Aplite
uses: feldspar feed for ceramics and glass
entries.notes: Sugary, pale, granite-composition dikes: the opposite end of the pegmatite family. Mined for ceramic feldspar.

entries.name: Nepheline syenite
entries.notes: Silica-undersaturated cousin of syenite; high alumina and alkalis make it a premium feed for glass and ceramics (e.g. Blue Mountain, Ontario).

entries.name: Peridotite
entries.notes: The bulk of Earth's upper mantle; exposed in ophiolites. Oman's ophiolite is a test bed for locking CO2 into carbonate rock.

entries.name: Dunite
entries.notes: Nearly pure olivine. Its refractory nature lines steel furnaces; gem peridot comes from peridotite and dunite.

entries.name: Pyroxenite
entries.notes: The mafic complement to peridotite in the mantle; carried up in volcanic xenoliths, giving direct samples of tens of kilometres down.

entries.name: Komatiite
entries.notes: Ultra-hot Archean lava (1600°C+), almost never seen after 2.5 billion years ago; spinifex crystal texture. Hosts the great Kambalda nickel sulphide ores.

entries.name: Kimberlite
entries.weathers_to: friable 'blue ground', then yellow ground clay
entries.notes: Volcanic pipes blasted up from 150+ km depth, named after Kimberley, South Africa — essentially the only economic primary source of diamonds.

entries.name: Lamproite
entries.notes: Ultrapotassic cousin of kimberlite. The Argyle pipe in Western Australia was the world's main source of pink diamonds (closed 2020).

entries.name: Carbonatite
uses: rare earth elements (Mountain Pass, Bayan Obo)
entries.notes: The coolest lava on Earth (~540°C): Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania is the only volcano erupting carbonatite today. Major REE and niobium source.

entries.name: Lamprophyre
entries.notes: Dark, mica-heavy dikes. Cross-cutting lamprophyre dikes give minimum ages for the events they cut; some accompany orogenic gold.

entries.name: Nephelinite
entries.notes: Silica-undersaturated dark lava of ocean islands and the East African Rift; chemically opposite to rhyolite. Nepheline syenite is its plutonic twin.

entries.name: Boninite
entries.notes: Rare high-magnesium but silica-saturated magma of young subduction forearcs; found in the Izu-Bonin and Mariana forearcs. A window into how arcs started.

entries.name: Volcanic breccia
entries.notes: Angular fragments torn from vent walls and welded by ash. Cascade volcanoes shed lahar breccias far downstream of the cone.

entries.name: Pitchstone
entries.notes: Glassy rhyolite with 1-10% water, with a greasy resinous lustre; devitrifies with age and is the parent of perlite when finely cracked.
